name: Retinaldehyde (Retinal)

lead: Retinaldehyde (retinal) is a form of vitamin A that sits one step from retinoic acid, the active retinoid in prescription tretinoin. In skincare it is sold over the counter as a step between retinol and tretinoin, for smoother skin, fewer wrinkles and more even tone.

Skin converts retinal into retinoic acid, which acts on retinoid receptors to change cell turnover and gene expression, and supports collagen. Skin-specific studies are few: an exploratory 1999 trial in facial rosacea, a 1999 human tolerance study, and a registered split-face study of 56 people with aging skin.

paras: People apply it as a serum or cream, usually at night, and often alternate it with stronger prescription retinoids while skin adjusts. Results in texture and tone build over weeks to months, with sunscreen used by day.

No published data in the sources quantify irritation for retinal on skin, though retinoids in general can cause dryness, redness and peeling. Retinal is chemically reactive and oxidizes readily, so product stability matters. Retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy.

chain: Converts to retinoic acid in skin
angle.text: Retinal is an over-the-counter retinoid that skin converts into retinoic acid, which speeds cell turnover and supports collagen for smoother, more even skin. It is used as a middle step between retinol and prescription tretinoin, and skin-specific human studies are few.

lead: Retinaldehyde, usually called retinal, is the aldehyde form of vitamin A. In skincare it is sold in over-the-counter serums and creams as a retinoid positioned between retinol and prescription tretinoin: it sits one enzymatic step from retinoic acid, the active molecule that drives skin renewal.[1][2][3] People use it to work on fine lines, uneven texture, dullness and pigmentation associated with photoaging, and to even out skin tone as part of a routine aimed at a smoother, clearer complexion.

In the body, retinol and retinal do not signal directly; they are converted to retinoic acid in target tissues as needed, and retinoic acid acts on retinoic acid receptors and retinoid X receptors to regulate gene expression.[2][4] Because retinal needs only one conversion step, proponents describe it as acting faster and more gently than retinol, and brands often market it for people whose skin is sensitive to stronger retinoids.[3]

Retinal is also the light-absorbing molecule of vision, and most of the biomedical literature using the word is about the eye: 11-cis-retinal binds opsin proteins, and its light-triggered change of shape starts the visual cycle.[4][1] The skin research is a smaller body of work, including a 1999 exploratory study in rosacea, a 1999 tolerance review with a long-term pilot, a randomized trial of 0.05% and 0.1% creams in photoaged skin and a split-face comparison of a retinal formulation with retinol.[5][6][7] A split-face study of stabilized retinaldehyde in aging skin is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov.[8]

In looksmaxxing forums retinal is mentioned occasionally as a gentler retinoid, sometimes alongside prescription options such as tazarotene.[9] Wikipedia's photoaging article notes that tretinoin is the best-studied topical for sun-damaged skin, with over-the-counter retinol and retinal products studied less.[10]
infobox: Visual chromophore; intermediate between retinol and retinoic acid [4]

paras: Retinal is formulated into face serums and creams for photoaged skin: fine lines, rough texture, dullness and uneven pigmentation. Randomized trials in Korean volunteers measured wrinkle depth, hydration, transepidermal water loss and the melanin index, which are the same features people try to improve with retinoids.[6]

Retinoids in general are used topically for acne, psoriasis and photoaging, and retinol and retinal are described as vitamin A forms rather than direct receptor agonists.[2] Brands position retinal for users who want a stronger effect than retinol with less irritation than prescription retinoic acid; the published comparisons described below are small.[5][6]

The 1999 rosacea study tested a 0.05% retinaldehyde cream applied once daily for six months in women with persistent erythema and telangiectasia, prompted by anecdotal reports that retinoic acid helps mild rosacea.[7]

Wikipedia sorts retinoids into generations. The vitamin A forms (retinol, retinal and their esters) are not directly active signalling molecules; first-generation retinoids are the naturally active retinoic acids (tretinoin, isotretinoin, alitretinoin); the third generation includes adapalene and tazarotene; the fourth, trifarotene, was approved in the US in 2019.[2] On that scale retinal is the nearest vitamin A form to the active acid.[2][4]

Retinol has been used in over-the-counter cosmetics since 1984, and Wikipedia reports that in the EU and UK retinol has been regulated as a cosmetic ingredient since November 2025, with concentration limits and mandatory labelling.[3] Those limits are described for retinol; the article does not say how retinal is treated.

Tretinoin was developed for acne at the University of Pennsylvania in the 1960s by James Fulton and Albert Kligman and was approved by the FDA for that purpose in 1971; it is described as the most-studied retinoid for sun-damaged skin, increasing collagen production with visible results over weeks to months.[11]

Retinal has a beta-ionone ring joined to a polyene chain ending in an aldehyde group; the all-trans and 11-cis isomers are the biologically important ones.[1] The aldehyde makes it chemically reactive, prone to oxidation and to forming Schiff bases, so formulations are protected from air and light.[1] Wikipedia notes that retinol is likewise easily degraded by light, oxygen and heat, and that formulators have explored derivatives, antioxidants and delivery systems to stabilise it.[3]

Animals make retinal from dietary carotenoids such as beta-carotene or take it in from animal foods; some carnivores cannot convert carotenoids at all. It interconverts reversibly with retinol, the transport and storage form of vitamin A, and can be oxidized to retinoic acid by retinal dehydrogenases.[4] Retinoic acid is a signalling molecule that binds retinoic acid receptors and retinoid X receptors.[4][1]

In the eye, 11-cis-retinal is the chromophore bound to opsin proteins; light converts it to all-trans-retinal and starts the visual cycle, which is regenerated by an enzymatic pathway split between rod outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium cells. George Wald and colleagues had outlined this cycle by 1958, and Wald shared the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.[4] The molecule was first called retinene and later renamed vitamin A aldehyde.[4] Some microbes also use retinal in their own light-sensing rhodopsins.[4]

Tolerance. A 1999 paper in Dermatology reviewed published and unpublished data on topical retinaldehyde and added a long-term pilot of 45 patients who used it on the face for 12 to 89 months. The authors concluded it was better tolerated than retinoic acid, suited sensitive facial skin, had no phototoxic or photoallergic properties, and was not associated with side effects in long-term use.[5][6]

Rosacea. In an exploratory 1999 study, women with vascular signs of facial rosacea applied a 0.05% retinaldehyde cream once daily for six months, with clinical and instrumental assessment of erythema and telangiectasia.[7]

Photoaging. A 2018 randomized, double-blind trial in 40 Korean women compared 0.1% and 0.05% retinaldehyde creams applied twice daily for three months. About 95 percent of each group showed overall improvement; both strengths improved texture, hydration and transepidermal water loss without a significant difference between them, while only the 0.1% cream significantly improved the melanin index. Both were reported as well tolerated.[6]

Versus retinol. A 2021 randomized, split-face, investigator-blinded study in 23 Korean volunteers compared a multilamellar-vesicle retinaldehyde formulation with retinol over eight weeks. Wrinkle depth and other measures improved on both sides, with the retinaldehyde side improving more on most measures but not dermal density; no adverse events were attributed to either cream.[6]

Aging skin. A split-face study of stabilized retinaldehyde in skin aging and photoaging (56 participants, started 2023) is registered as completed on ClinicalTrials.gov.[8] Other studies listed in indexes under related terms concern retinal as an eye structure and do not involve topical skin products.

Retinoids that act as receptor agonists can raise triglycerides and cholesterol in oral use, and oral retinoids can cause serious fetal defects; Wikipedia advises that women of childbearing potential avoid oral retinoids unless they take pregnancy-prevention steps, and notes that topical tretinoin is not recommended in the first trimester as a precaution, although a 2026 Nordic cohort study found no increase in birth defects.[2] Dietary retinol and retinal are normal, and are linked to birth defects only in deficiency or excess.[2]

The most common problem with topical retinoids is retinoid dermatitis, with redness, scaling, dryness and itching.[3] The retinaldehyde trials above reported good tolerance in their samples, which were small and mostly short.[5][6] Retinoid products are commonly accompanied by sun-protection advice, and sun protection is the main prevention strategy for photoaging.[10]

On looksmax.org, one user asked about alternating leftover retinal with tazarotene each night while skin adjusted to the prescription retinoid; a reply advised using only the tazarotene.[9] The thread also asks about obtaining prescription retinoids from overseas pharmacies.[9] The wiki does not reproduce application schedules.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org retinal is mentioned occasionally as a gentler option used alongside or before stronger retinoids [9]. Most skincare discussion of it appears in general retinoid conversations.
